growth.label: Economic growth
growth.what: How fast the country's economy grew after inflation (real GDP).
growth.why: Growth creates jobs and income. Shrinking or stalled output is the most basic sign of trouble.

inflation.label: Inflation
inflation.what: How much consumer prices rose over the year (yearly average).
inflation.why: Moderate inflation (around 2%) is normal. High inflation erodes savings and wages; falling prices can signal weak demand.

unemployment.label: Unemployment
unemployment.what: The share of people in the labor force without a job. Reported for fewer countries.
unemployment.why: High unemployment wastes talent and income. Very low can mean a tight labor market.

debt.label: Government debt
debt.what: Everything the national government owes, compared with a year of the country's output.
debt.why: More debt means more of tomorrow's income goes to interest, and less room to respond to a crisis.

ca.label: Current account
ca.what: The balance of a country's trade and income with the world. Negative means it borrows from abroad to pay its way.
ca.why: Large, lasting deficits make a country depend on foreign lenders, which can end suddenly.

fiscal.label: Government budget balance
fiscal.what: Government spending minus revenue in a year. Negative means a deficit.
fiscal.why: Persistent big deficits add to debt and can force higher taxes, cuts or inflation.

gdppc.label: Income per person
gdppc.what: Economic output per person at market exchange rates.
gdppc.why: A rough guide to average living standards. It is shown for context and is not part of the score.

gdp.label: Size of economy
gdp.what: Total economic output in US dollars.
gdp.why: Shows how big the economy is. Not part of the score.

pop.label: Population
pop.why: Context. Not part of the score.

interest.label: Interest on government debt
interest.what: The share of what the government collects that goes straight to paying interest on its debt.
interest.why: Interest is money that cannot fund schools, roads or defense. When it takes a large share, the debt is becoming a burden.

reserves.label: Foreign reserves
reserves.what: Foreign currency and gold the central bank holds, measured by how many months of imports they could pay for.
reserves.why: Reserves are a cushion in a crisis. Under 3 months is thin; countries with no reserves run out first when money flees.

extdebt.label: Foreign debt payments
extdebt.what: Payments on debt owed to foreigners, compared with what the country earns from exports. Reported for developing countries.
extdebt.why: Foreign debt must be paid in foreign money. A high share of export income going to it is a classic warning sign.

gov.label: Rule of law
gov.what: World Bank index of how far people trust and follow the rules: courts, contracts, property rights, police. About -2.5 (weak) to +2.5 (strong).
gov.why: Investors, businesses and lenders need to trust that contracts hold. It is the best single predictor of how a country handles stress.

geff.label: Government effectiveness
geff.what: World Bank index of the quality of public services and how well policy is carried out. About -2.5 to +2.5.
geff.why: A government that cannot deliver cannot fix a crisis.

lifeexp.label: Life expectancy
lifeexp.what: How long a baby born today is expected to live.
lifeexp.why: Health and income show up in how long people live. It captures living standards that GDP misses.

gdppp.label: Income per person (price-adjusted)
gdppp.what: Output per person adjusted for what money buys locally (purchasing-power prices).
gdppp.why: Market exchange rates understate what people in poorer countries can buy. This is a fairer guide to living standards.

govq.label: Governance
govq.what: World Bank index of how far people trust and follow the rules: courts, contracts, property rights, police. About -2.5 (weak) to +2.5 (strong).
govq.why: Investors, businesses and lenders need to trust that contracts hold. It is the best single predictor of how a country handles stress.

borrow.label: Borrowing strength
borrow.what: How easily the country can fund itself: its institutions, its income, and whether it borrows in a major world currency.
borrow.why: The US and Japan can carry debt that would sink most countries, because the world wants to lend to them. This reading captures that.

growth.label: Growth
growth.rule: Full marks at 6% or more, 65 at 2%, 35 at 0%, zero at -4% or worse.

inflation.label: Inflation
inflation.rule: Best at 1% to 3%. 70 at 5%, 30 at 10%, near zero at 20% or more. Falling prices also lose points.

unemployment.label: Unemployment
unemployment.rule: Full marks at 3% or less, 65 at 8%, 20 at 15%, zero at 25%.

debt.label: Government debt
debt.rule: Full marks under 30% of GDP, 55 at 90%, 30 at 120%, 10 at 150%.

fiscal.label: Budget balance
fiscal.rule: Full marks at balance or surplus, 70 at -5% of GDP, 10 at -12%.

interest.label: Interest on debt
interest.rule: Full marks under 3% of revenue, 60 at 15%, 30 at 25%, near zero at 40% or more.

borrow.label: Borrowing strength
borrow.rule: How easily the country can fund itself: half rule of law and government effectiveness, a quarter income per person, and a quarter for borrowing in a major world currency (dollar, euro, yen, pound, Swiss franc).

ca.label: Current account
ca.rule: Best from about 0% to +10% of GDP. 45 at -6%, 10 at -12% or worse.

reserves.label: Foreign reserves
reserves.rule: Full marks at 9 months of imports or more, 55 at 3 months, 35 at 2, zero at half a month. Countries that borrow in a world currency need fewer.

extdebt.label: Foreign debt payments
extdebt.rule: Full marks under 5% of exports, 55 at 20%, 25 at 30%, zero at 50% or more.

currency.label: Currency vs. the dollar
currency.rule: Based on how much more of the local currency a dollar buys than a year ago. Full marks if it held or rose; 65 at a 10% fall; zero at 60%.

govq.label: Governance
govq.rule: Average of rule of law and government effectiveness (-2.5 to +2.5). Full marks at +1.8, 55 at 0, 25 at -1, zero at -2 or worse.

lifeexp.label: Life expectancy
lifeexp.rule: Full marks at 83 years, 90 at 78, 60 at 70, 25 at 60, zero at 50 or less.

rules._method: The score is 80% a weighted average of every reading below plus 20% the weakest of four areas (activity, public finances, external strength, institutions and people), so one badly broken area drags it down harder than a good one lifts it. Missing readings are skipped (at least six are needed). Countries with thin or unreliable numbers are flagged low confidence.
